theorem.title: Uniform exclusion of Landau–Siegel zeros
theorem.statement: There is an absolute constant c > 0 such that every real zero β ∈ (0,1) of every primitive nonprincipal real Dirichlet L-function of conductor q ≥ 3 satisfies (1 − β) log q ≥ c.
theorem.scopeNote: This is the real-zero logarithmic gap. It does not give a zero-free half-plane, a numerical value of c, or the stronger quasi-Riemann statements.
theorem.sourceNote: Statement paraphrased from the OpenAI paper, Theorem 1. The linked sources retain their original wording.

versions.label: OpenAI
versions.title: Uniform exclusion of Landau–Siegel zeros
versions.aiAssistance: OpenAI release; upstream Lean solution in the OpenAI math repository
versions.summary: The original short proof. A real zero close to 1 forces a shortage of primes with χ(p)=1; the complementary primes feed a weighted determinant whose Archimedean size is smaller than its forced p-adic divisibility.
versions.changeSummary: Origin of this lineage. It proves the real-zero gap but gives no numerical value for c.

lean.label: OAI.NumberTheory.SiegelZeros.Main
lean.note: The solution module exists upstream. The comparator file SiegelZeros.lean is a challenge statement ending in `sorry`; the solution module is the proof. Proofweave has not re-run the kernel or the comparator.

proofSteps.label: Theorem 1 · uniform real-zero gap
proofSteps.detail: Every real zero β ∈ (0,1) of a primitive nonprincipal real Dirichlet L-function of conductor q ≥ 3 satisfies (1 − β) log q ≥ c for an absolute c > 0.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 2 · prime bias
proofSteps.detail: A real zero close to 1 forces a shortage of primes with χ(p)=1. For X ≥ 3, the sum over χ(p)=1 is bounded by ℓ + δ(log X)²/ℓ; the primes with χ(p)=−1 carry the remaining logarithmic mass.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 3 · interpolation on a projected box
proofSteps.detail: For a surjective A: C⁴ → C³ whose kernel is spanned by a Q-linearly independent vector, monomials of bounded separate degrees evaluate surjectively on the projected integer box.

proofSteps.label: Corollary 4 · spanning rows
proofSteps.detail: Rows with degrees α₁ ≤ 32H²ᐟ³U and α₂, α₃ ≤ 32H⁻¹ᐟ³U span the evaluation space.

proofSteps.label: §4 · weighted determinant
proofSteps.detail: Order rows by α₁ + Hα₂ + Hα₃, retain a spanning subset, and form a nonzero determinant Δ. Lemma 6 gives S₁ ≥ c₀MH²ᐟ³U and S₂ ≤ C₀MH⁻¹ᐟ³U.

proofSteps.label: §5 · Archimedean bound
proofSteps.detail: Hadamard's inequality bounds |N(Δ)| from above using the four complex embeddings of the biquadratic field.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 7 · p-adic divisibility
proofSteps.detail: For primes p with χ(p)=−1, Frobenius congruence and the row-replacement identity force p^{E_p} | Δ. Taking norms gives the lower bound.

proofSteps.label: §6 · parameter assembly
proofSteps.detail: Choose H so S₂/S₁ ≤ 1/12 and a large fixed γ with N = ⌈q^γ⌉. Combining the two bounds gives 1 ≤ 13/16 + 1/16 = 7/8, a contradiction.

versions.label: Banks
versions.title: On the OpenAI proof that Landau–Siegel zeros do not exist
versions.method: Direct proof with explicit constants; same interpolation determinant
versions.aiAssistance: Claude used for an initial report and draft; the author rewrote and verified every line
versions.summary: A line-by-line exposition of the OpenAI argument with explicit constants q₀ = 10¹⁰ and δ₀ = 3.0 × 10⁻³, plus a dependency diagram. The author explicitly claims no new ideas.
versions.changeSummary: Not a shorter proof: it trades brevity for explicit constants, direct contradiction, and a readable dependency graph.

lean.label: No upstream Lean artifact found
lean.note: This prototype found no Lean formalization of the Banks exposition. The upstream solution formalizes the OpenAI route, not this explicit-constant presentation.

proofSteps.label: Theorem 1.1 · explicit gap
proofSteps.detail: There are absolute q₀ ≥ 9 and δ₀ > 0 such that every primitive real Dirichlet character of conductor q ≥ q₀ and every real zero β ∈ (0,1) satisfy (1 − β) log q ≥ δ₀. One can take q₀ = 10¹⁰ and δ₀ = 3.0 × 10⁻³.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 2.1 · prime bias
proofSteps.detail: A zero with δ = (1 − β) log q small forces χ(p)=−1 for most primes. The lemma makes the loss explicit with constants C₁ and C₂.

proofSteps.label: §3 · interpolation chain
proofSteps.detail: Lemma 3.1 nearest point → Lemma 3.2 faces of a polytope → Lemma 3.3 nonvanishing on Z⁴ → Proposition 3.4 interpolation → Corollary 3.5 spanning rows.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 4.1 · greedy selection
proofSteps.detail: Order rows by weight and retain a row exactly when it increases the span. The retained rows form a nonzero determinant Δ.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 4.2 · S₁ and S₂₃
proofSteps.detail: The retained rows put almost all degree in the first variable: S₁ ≥ N⁴M and S₂₃ ≤ S₁/12 for a suitable fixed H.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 5.1 · upper bound
proofSteps.detail: Every conjugate of θₙ is below 8N√q; Hadamard's inequality gives the Archimedean upper bound for |N(Δ)|.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 6.1 · Frobenius congruence
proofSteps.detail: For odd p with χ(p)=−1, θᵖ ≡ g_p(θ) mod pZ[a,b], where g_p is σ or στ. This is the congruence that makes the determinant divisible.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 6.2 · prime powers in Δ
proofSteps.detail: Row replacement preserves Δ and shows p^{E_p} | Δ for each admissible prime p > H.

proofSteps.label: Corollary 6.3 · lower bound
proofSteps.detail: Summing the prime-power divisibility over p ≤ M gives the p-adic lower bound for |N(Δ)|.

versions.label: Kerr
versions.title: A simpler proof that there are no Landau–Siegel zeros
versions.aiAssistance: ChatGPT assisted with the mathematical development and preparation; Banks shared a draft of his exposition
versions.summary: Replaces the interpolation and determinant analysis with a pigeonhole argument that finds a bounded-degree polynomial vanishing modulo many primes. Masser's zero estimate contradicts the degree bound.
versions.changeSummary: Removes the interpolation lemma, greedy selection, and determinant construction. It keeps the biquadratic field and adds Masser's theorem as the nonvanishing input.

lean.label: No upstream Lean artifact found
lean.note: This prototype found no Lean formalization of Kerr's pigeonhole/Masser proof.

proofSteps.label: Theorem 1 · no Landau–Siegel zeros
proofSteps.detail: There is an absolute c > 0 such that every real zero β ∈ (0,1) of every primitive nonprincipal real Dirichlet L-function of conductor q satisfies (1 − β) log |q| ≥ c.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 1 · prime bias
proofSteps.detail: For X ≥ 3, the sum of log p / p over primes with χ(p)=1 is ≪ log|q| + (1−β)(log X)².

proofSteps.label: Lemma 2 · alternative basis
proofSteps.detail: The polynomials G_{i,j,k} = x₁^v (x₁^p − x_ℓ)^e x₂^j x₃^k form a triangular basis of the lattice L_D.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 3 · counting polynomials
proofSteps.detail: The number of coefficient vectors with bounded height is at least the product of the coordinate-box sizes.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 4 · vanishing modulo primes
proofSteps.detail: For a finite set of primes with χ(p)=−1, the number of possible value vectors modulo P is at most P^{4r} ∏ p^{−4E_p}.

proofSteps.label: Lemma 5 · bounded-degree polynomial
proofSteps.detail: If the primes with χ(p)=−1 carry enough mass, pigeonhole produces a nonzero F ∈ L_D vanishing at every grid point.

proofSteps.label: Masser's zero estimate
proofSteps.detail: Masser's theorem gives deg F ≥ ((N−1)/3)^{4/3}. Lemma 7 supplies μ(π(Z⁴)) ≥ 4/3, so deg F > D, contradicting F ∈ L_D.

versions.label: Green
versions.title: On Landau–Siegel zeros
versions.aiAssistance: ChatGPT 6 Astra “vibemathing” session; rewritten by the author; no human originality claimed
versions.summary: Avoids the biquadratic field entirely. A Gram matrix is nonsingular because the rows are independent; resultants prove row independence, and the Archimedean and p-adic bounds compare the determinant.
versions.changeSummary: Removes the biquadratic field and the interpolation lemma. It replaces them with a Gram-matrix/resultant argument in Q(√d).

lean.label: No upstream Lean artifact found
lean.note: This prototype found no Lean formalization of Green's Q(√d) Gram/resultant proof.

proofSteps.label: Theorem 1.1 · prime sum bound
proofSteps.detail: With X := q^C, the sum of log p / p over primes p ≤ X with χ(p)=−1 is at most (1/2 + O(1/C)) log X + O_C(1).

proofSteps.label: Lemma 3.1 · row independence
proofSteps.detail: If the points satisfy a Schwarz–Zippel bound and nJ > 2RS + J(R+S), the rows v_{r,s} are linearly independent. The proof factors a polynomial and uses resultants.

proofSteps.label: §4 · Hadamard bound
proofSteps.detail: The entries of v_{r,s} are bounded by RJ(2N√q)^{r+s}; Hadamard gives log det G ≤ R²S(1/2 + O(1/C)) log X + O(X³).

proofSteps.label: §5 · p-adic valuation
proofSteps.detail: If χ(p)=−1, the Frobenius relation z^p ≡ z′ shows that p^{e_p} divides det G, with e_p bounded below by the row count.

proofSteps.label: §2 · determinant comparison
proofSteps.detail: Since det G is a positive integer, the product of the prime powers divides it. Comparing the lower and upper bounds gives Theorem 1.1.

versions.label: Barreto
versions.title: An elementary proof of the non-existence of Landau–Siegel zeros
versions.aiAssistance: GPT-6 Astra proposed the simplification and checked the text
versions.summary: A 3-page variant of Green's proof. The Wronskian of the polynomial basis proves row independence; Frobenius congruence gives divisibility, and the determinant bounds prove the prime-sum estimate and the real-zero corollary.
versions.changeSummary: Removes Green's resultant calculation and replaces it with a Wronskian. The paper says the proof is suitable for an introductory course in analytic number theory.

lean.label: No upstream Lean artifact found
lean.note: No Lean formalization of Barreto's 3-page Wronskian proof was found. The upstream Lean solution follows the longer OpenAI route.

versions.sourceLabel: 3-page manuscript shared as images on X; cited by van Dijk (Hexagon:2610.00409v2)

proofSteps.label: Theorem 1 · prime sum bound
proofSteps.detail: Uniformly for x ≥ 2, the sum of log p / p over p ≤ x with χ(p)=−1 is at most (1/2) log x + (1/4) log q + log log(3x) + O(1).

proofSteps.label: Chebyshev + Mertens
proofSteps.detail: The proof uses Chebyshev's bound, Mertens' estimate, and the elementary prime-counting bounds recorded in Montgomery–Vaughan.

proofSteps.label: Wronskian row independence
proofSteps.detail: The rows are indexed by monomials z^r w^s. Their Wronskian has degree < ℓx; the determinant of the leading coefficients is nonzero because the polynomials a!(t choose a) have distinct degrees. Hence the rows are independent.

proofSteps.label: Frobenius congruence
proofSteps.detail: For an odd prime p with χ(p)=−1, α_i^p ≡ ᾱ_i (mod pZ[√d]). Thus z^p − w vanishes at every point, and every positive z-derivative is divisible by p.

proofSteps.label: p-adic divisibility
proofSteps.detail: Replace z^r w^s by z^{r−ph}(z^p − w)^h w^s. The replacement is unitriangular, preserves the minor D, and forces p^{Σ⌊r/p⌋} | D.

proofSteps.label: Determinant size bound
proofSteps.detail: Both conjugates of every entry are bounded by B = 2√(2x) q^{1/4}. The determinant expansion, the prime divisibility, and the choice k = ⌊log² B⌋ give the final bound.

proofSteps.label: Corollary 2 · real zeros
proofSteps.detail: Partial summation, Jensen's inequality, the Euler product, and the Hadamard product give (1 − β) log q ≥ 1 − O(log log(3q)/log q), hence an absolute c > 0.

versions.label: van Dijk
versions.title: A Frobenius determinant proof of the non-existence of Landau–Siegel zeros
versions.aiAssistance: GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5; the author attributes the new arguments to the models
versions.summary: Follows Kerr, Green, and Barreto. Reduction modulo the largest inert prime turns nonvanishing into a polynomial root count, replacing both resultants and Wronskians.
versions.changeSummary: A recombination branch: it keeps the Frobenius determinant idea but replaces the row-independence tool with a root count, and gets an effective asymptotic constant.

lean.label: No upstream Lean artifact found
lean.note: This prototype found no Lean formalization of van Dijk's root-count proof.

proofSteps.label: Theorem 1 · prime sum bound
proofSteps.detail: There is an absolute effective C such that I_d(x) ≤ (1/2) log x + (1/4) log|d| + log log(3x) + C.

proofSteps.label: Nonvanishing via root count
proofSteps.detail: Modulo the largest inert prime R, a row dependence would produce a nonzero polynomial of degree < RS with R distinct roots of multiplicity ≥ S, impossible.

proofSteps.label: Frobenius divisibility
proofSteps.detail: For an odd inert prime p, z^p − w vanishes at the chosen points; row replacement gives p^{2E_p} | N.

proofSteps.label: Size comparison
proofSteps.detail: The determinant expansion and the prime-power lower bound are compared; Appendix A supplies the numerical estimates for the explicit constant.

proofSteps.label: Corollary 1 · real zeros
proofSteps.detail: Every real zero β ∈ (0,1) of a primitive nonprincipal real Dirichlet character satisfies (1 − β) log q ≥ 1 − O(log log(3q)/log q), hence an absolute effective c > 0.

versions.label: OpenAI · 11/12
versions.title: The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis (alternate 11/12 proof)
versions.summary: Proves a zero-free half-plane Re(s) > 11/12 for all Dirichlet L-functions and finite-order Hecke L-functions over Q(√−3). It implies the real-zero gap but proves a stronger theorem by a different method.
versions.changeSummary: Not a simplification of the 3-page proof. It is a stronger theorem on a separate track.

lean.label: No separate Lean artifact for the 11/12 proof
lean.note: The upstream 7/8 formalization is a stronger statement but not a formalization of this 11/12 proof.

proofSteps.label: Theorem 1.1 · Re(s) > 11/12
proofSteps.detail: Every finite-order Hecke L-function over Q(√−3), and hence every Dirichlet L-function, has no zeros in Re(s) > 11/12.

proofSteps.label: Mean-square estimate
proofSteps.detail: A power-saving mean-square estimate for twisted Möbius sums is the analytic input.

proofSteps.label: Poisson summation / dual mean square
proofSteps.detail: Poisson summation produces cubic Gauss sums and a dual mean-square estimate.

proofSteps.label: Iteration of the dual estimate
proofSteps.detail: Iterate the dual mean-square estimate to complete the mean-square bound.

proofSteps.label: Transfer to Dirichlet L-functions
proofSteps.detail: Transfer the Hecke half-plane to Dirichlet L-functions by composing with the norm and factoring the L-function.

versions.method: Common continuation principle + sextic large sieve

versions.summary: Proves the strongest half-plane in this release: Re(s) > 7/8 for all Dirichlet L-functions and finite-order Hecke L-functions over Q(√−3). It implies the real-zero gap but is a different, much stronger theorem.
versions.changeSummary: Not the old version of the 3-page proof. It is a stronger theorem on a separate track; comparing page counts across tracks is misleading.

proofSteps.label: Theorem 1.1 · Re(s) > 7/8
proofSteps.detail: Every finite-order Hecke L-function over Q(√−3), and hence every Dirichlet L-function, has no zeros in Re(s) > 7/8, with the principal pole at s = 1 allowed.

proofSteps.label: Common continuation principle
proofSteps.detail: A common continuation principle compares a normalized character sum with a Mellin integral containing 1/L.

proofSteps.label: Completed sum and cubic reflection
proofSteps.detail: The completed sum has a reflection representation and a Poisson representation.

proofSteps.label: Poisson representation and Euler factors
proofSteps.detail: The Poisson representation expresses each row through a quotient of Hecke L-functions and a controlled Euler product.

proofSteps.label: Zero detector with saturated witnesses
proofSteps.detail: A zero detector assigns zero-free rectangles and produces large Dirichlet polynomials.

proofSteps.label: Sextic large sieve
proofSteps.detail: A sextic large sieve counts the relevant rows.

proofSteps.label: Compensated probe and inverse moment
proofSteps.detail: Part II introduces prime compensation, asymmetric scales, and inverse-moment estimates to move the boundary from 11/12 to 7/8.
